Peace around the Mediterranean Sea is the broad theme of Resolution A/69/80, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The lands that ring the sea, the text holds, bear the chief duty for its peace, safety, and joint work. It welcomes the steps of Euro-Mediterranean states to deepen their ties, above all in the fight against terror, through the joint code agreed at Barcelona in 2005.

Past pledges and meetings of the shore states are recalled in force. A fresh push came in 2008, when the Paris summit launched a stronger pact, the Union for the Mediterranean. The vote keeps the sea's peace framed as a shared task, from Gibraltar to the Levant.

frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d180: The Secret Protocol of the Moscow Conference, dated November 1, 1943, is Document 180 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d280:
The United States Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 404 at Cairo on 22 November 1943, the proposed American agenda for the Sextant Conference. It is the detailed counterpart to the shorter British agenda printed next in the volume, and it lays out five heads of business.

After procedure and the overall objective, the European and Mediterranean head calls for enemy estimates, bomber offensive and anti-U-boat reports, the Azores facilities, and readiness reports on Overlord, Rankin, and Jupiter. The Japan head asks for a 1944 enemy estimate, a short-term plan for Japan's defeat, and reports on Southeast Asia, China, and the Pacific. A final head weighs resources against plans, asking whether the forces exist to carry out everything proposed.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d380: An editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume covers the Tehran dinner meeting of 1 December 1943, which lasted, by the President's Log, until half past ten at night. No official minutes of the conversation appear to have been prepared at the time. A memorandum written by Charles Bohlen a few days later indicates two things. The Declaration on Iran and the conference communiqué were discussed at the dinner. They were also put into final form there. The editors print this note in place of a contemporary record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d480:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on December 4, 1943, the day the Second Cairo Conference opened. Hull remained in Washington while Roosevelt met Churchill at Cairo, fresh from Tehran. The cable appears in the State Department's published Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Hull's cables were the department's way of sitting at a conference it had not attended in person. They brought Washington's news and views to the President at the moment decisions were being made abroad. For the reader, this message is part of the long-distance conversation that tied the traveling summit to the home government throughout December 1943.
frus-1944-quebec-d80:
Riddleberger wrote to Secretary of State Hull on September 4, 1944. He headed the Division of Central European Affairs at the department. His letter appears in the pre-conference papers of the Quebec 1944 volume. The conference in Canada opened eight days later.

A division chief reported upward as summit planning quickened. Central Europe faced occupation, new borders, and great human need. Hull needed his experts' judgment before advising the President. For readers, the letter shows the State Department's own chain at work. Regional specialists briefed their secretary while the Quebec agenda took shape.
frus-1944-quebec-d180:
An editors' note prints Harry Dexter White's memorandum of Roosevelt's talk with Morgenthau on September 13, 1944. White was not present; he summarized what the Treasury secretary told him. Roosevelt had summoned Morgenthau to Quebec to talk with Lord Cherwell, and over tea he went through the Treasury's book of memoranda on Germany item by item, setting limits on the discussion.

Morgenthau could discuss internationalizing the Ruhr and the Saar, including the Kiel Canal, Roosevelt said. He could even mention giving Holland a piece of western Germany for land the Germans had inundated. But occupation zones were a military question, and partitioning a political one; both were off limits. Eden was being sent for. "Don't worry about Churchill," the president added. "He is going to be tough too."

The Combined Chiefs approved sending the message to Eisenhower, and it went out as Facs 81.

Eisenhower was asked to review the situation carefully with the object of an early release of craft from Overlord. Regard was to be had for his build-up needs until adequate port facilities became available, and for the weather limits on using such craft in the near future. An early report on the matter was desired.

arxiv-2606-05080: Can an AI actually do research — plan experiments, run them, and engineer solutions over long horizons? AutoLab is a benchmark that asks exactly that of frontier models, testing them on extended autonomous research and engineering tasks. It measures the gap between today's AI assistants and a true AI scientist.
arxiv-2606-05180: Evaluating teaching quality from classroom data is usually a black box of scores. This paper compares SHAP values — a classic explanation technique — with LLM-generated rationales for rubric-based teaching assessment. The study asks which kind of explanation actually helps humans understand and trust an evaluation of teaching.
arxiv-2606-05280: Kaleidoscopes turn simple mirrors into intricate patterns; this paper finds a mathematical cousin of that magic. It connects kaleidoscopic symmetry structures to wave equations through the prepotential — a master function encoding a theory's dynamics. The work reveals how reflection symmetries can generate the rich structure of physical theories.
arxiv-2606-05380: Online algorithms must decide now with incomplete information, and machine-learned predictions can help — if you do not trust them blindly. This paper studies learning-augmented online minimization with dual predictions: two forecasts whose disagreement signals caution. The framework gets the best of both worlds, fast when predictions are right and safe when they are wrong.
arxiv-2606-05480: A control algorithm tuned in simulation can fail on a real vehicle whose dynamics differ. CAPE evaluates control algorithm performance under learned vehicle dynamics models — testing controllers against data-driven stand-ins for the real car. Realistic evaluation before road testing saves money and prevents dangerous surprises.
arxiv-2606-05780: The WISE space telescope mapped the whole sky in infrared, seeing the heat of galaxies. This paper presents WISE photometry — precise brightness measurements — for galaxies within 10 megaparsecs, our cosmic neighborhood. The catalog gives astronomers a uniform infrared portrait of every nearby galaxy.
arxiv-2606-06080: Max@K policy gradients train agents to produce their best of K attempts — but estimating advantages there is tricky. This paper develops advantage estimates for that setting, correcting the bias that naive estimates introduce. Correct credit assignment keeps best-of-K training honest.
arxiv-2606-06280: Stochastic monotone inclusions generalize optimization to noisy, set-valued problems. This paper develops second-order splitting dynamics for them with closed-loop distribution — dynamics that adapt to their own randomness. The theory gives practitioners faster, steadier algorithms for uncertain problems. The methods handle noise without losing speed.
arxiv-2606-06380: Could consciousness emerge from AI agents inventing their own language to coordinate? This paper explores emergent language as an approach to conscious AI: when agents develop communication, something mind-like might follow. The proposal links the origins of language to the origins of experience.
arxiv-2606-06580: The next Galactic supernova will flood Earth with neutrinos — and DUNE, Hyper-Kamiokande, and JUNO will be watching. This paper shows how that flood reveals the neutrino mass ordering: which of the three types is heaviest. A dying star becomes the ultimate particle physics experiment.
arxiv-2606-06780: Moiré materials — stacked atomic sheets twisted at angles — host excitons that glow in revealing ways. This paper studies descriptor covariance and correlation hierarchy in moiré exciton photoluminescence. The hierarchy decodes what the light says about the quantum stacking.
arxiv-2606-06880: Agentic search — AI that searches like a researcher — needs to retrieve interaction spaces, not just documents. This paper moves toward retrieving those spaces. The shift could reinvent how agents find information. Interaction spaces capture the search process. The paradigm shift is overdue.
arxiv-2606-06980: Exchange interactions — the quantum glue of magnetism — shift under electric fields in layered metals. This paper tracks those trends in transition-metal trilayers. The control opens doors to electric-field-written magnetic memory. Trilayers are tunable magnetic sandwiches. Voltage controls the magnetism.
arxiv-2606-07080: A technical report on dots.tts — evidently a text-to-speech system — with minimal surviving metadata beyond its title. The report presumably documents the system's design or evaluation. Thin evidence limits what can be said confidently.  Technical reports document systems for posterity.
arxiv-2606-07180: Explaining vision models needs concepts that are minimal yet sufficient. OPTIMUS-Prime gives minimal and sufficient concept explanations for deep vision models. The explanations say exactly what matters, no more. Explanations should be minimal yet sufficient. Concept explanations beat feature attributions.
arxiv-2606-07380: Lifshitz multicriticality — where phases meet strangely — can be topologically enforced in one dimension. This paper shows how. The enforcement protects the criticality. Topological protection can stabilize critical phenomena. One-dimensional systems prove surprisingly rich. The theoretical result is striking.
tob-0144-56880:
After the sweeping systems of the first two volumes, volume three of The Secret Doctrine gathers looser material. Blavatsky left essays, fragments, and notes on occult history and symbolism, much of it unfinished at her death in 1891. Editors shaped the mass into a third volume.

Readers find teachings on hidden adepts, the inner meaning of symbols, and the secret history of religions. The tone shifts from chapter to chapter, since the pieces were written for different purposes. Fans prize the volume for hints dropped nowhere else. Newcomers fare better starting with volume one, then returning here.
tob-0180:
Cairo, 1904: Crowley said a voice named Aiwass dictated the Book of the Law to him over three days. The short, fierce text became the central scripture of Thelema, his new religion. Its best-known line lays down the law of the new age: do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the law.

Three chapters speak in the voices of Egyptian gods, mixing command, prophecy, and riddling verse. Followers treat each line as charged with meaning; critics see a curiosity of occult history. Either way, few short texts have founded so much. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry.
tob-9480:
Pindar, the leading lyric poet of ancient Greece, wrote odes to honor men who won at the Olympic Games. The Olympian Odes praise victors in running, wrestling, boxing, and chariot racing. Morice's English translation is the version named for this entry.

Each ode mixes praise of the winner with myths of gods and heroes linked to his city or family. Pindar warns winners to stay humble, since gods give success and can take it away. His grand, dense verse set the pattern for praise poetry in the West, and later poets from Horace onward studied him closely.
podcast-dannyjones-AziCjLnp780:
Dennis McKenna is a pharmacologist who has studied psychedelic plants for half a century, and the brother of the famed psychonaut Terence McKenna. With Danny Jones, he discusses the beings users of DMT report meeting in that drug's brief, intense state, and the ancient roots he traces for such encounters.

McKenna approaches the entities question as a scientist who has also had the experiences, which makes him an unusual witness. He separates what the chemistry does from what the visions mean, and refuses easy answers in both directions. Jones presses him on whether the beings are real. The episode preserves a serious researcher's fullest public thinking on a subject science mostly avoids, delivered with more honesty about uncertainty than either believers or skeptics usually allow.
podcast-dannyjones-EpW2lFqxx80:
Robert Salas was an Air Force officer stationed at a nuclear missile base in 1967 when, by his account, a glowing object hovered over the gate and his missiles went offline. On Danny Jones's podcast, the former nuclear warfare officer argues that something disturbing is still interfering with America's nuclear arsenal.

Salas has told his story to Congress and journalists for decades, and other veterans have reported similar shutdowns. The military's explanations differ, and no physical proof has settled the matter. What the episode offers is a trained officer's testimony, consistent over a lifetime, about the most sensitive weapons on earth. Jones questions him closely. Listeners must decide what such testimony is worth, which is exactly the problem the disclosure debate keeps circling.
podcast-dannyjones-LQZtTgA1N80:
Physicist Matthew Szydagis works on dark matter detection deep underground. He joins Danny Jones to discuss a startling extension of his field. It is evidence, as he presents it, that UFOs have been present on earth for a million years. His path runs from particle physics to the fossil and historical record of strange objects.

Szydagis applies a detector scientist's habits to fringe material, asking what would count as data and what is only story. Jones follows him from laboratory practice to ancient reports. The million-year claim is Szydagis's own reading, not his field's consensus, and the episode labels it by its framing. Listeners get something rare in this series: a working experimentalist explaining, carefully and on the record, why he thinks the UFO evidence deserves laboratory-grade attention.
podcast-joerogan-LeCpHugyI80:
Biogerontologist Aubrey de Grey joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 638, an early entry in the show's science run. De Grey argues that aging is a kind of damage the body can, in time, be repaired against. When this aired, the idea still sounded like science fiction to most ears.

He lays out the seven kinds of damage he wants medicine to fix, and his guess at the timeline. Rogan asks what a world without aging would do to work, family, and meaning. The episode preserves a bold claim at an early stage, from the man who made ending aging a public cause.
podcast-joerogan-RD-9Ghvt480:
Duncan Trussell's episode 1313 of the Joe Rogan Experience is another entry in the show's longest friendship. Trussell, comedian and host of a family-hour podcast of his own, treats Rogan's studio like a second home. Their talks need no news hook to get going.

The conversation drifts across psychedelic tales, the puzzle of the self, and the jokes Trussell builds from both. Rogan keeps one foot on the ground, telling his own stories between the flights. The episode is a pure example of the pair's chemistry, the blend of stand-up and soul talk that made Trussell a signature guest.
dawkins-early-man-in-britain-1880:
W. Boyd Dawkins published Early Man in Britain in 1880 as the sequel to his Cave Hunting of 1874. Its subtitle places man in the Tertiary period, the deep geological past. The book is a systematic survey of British Pleistocene geology, fauna, and human remains.

Dawkins orders the river gravels and cave deposits into one story of ice ages and shifting animal life. Into that frame he sets the flint tools and bones of Britain's first inhabitants. For decades the book was the standard account of early man in Britain. Its confidence is Victorian; its evidence base was the best then available. Later finds rewrote much, but the frame was his.
dawson-fossil-men-modern-representatives:
J. W. Dawson, a Canadian geologist and college principal, published Fossil Men in 1880. He reviewed the new fossil human finds coming out of Europe. Unlike many peers, he resisted Darwin's account of human descent.

Dawson argued for the recent origin and unity of the human race. He tried to fit caves, skulls, and tools within a biblical frame. His side lost the scientific argument that followed. The book matters now as a clear statement of the anti-Darwinian case by a serious geologist. Dawson wrote from his post at McGill, where he shaped Canadian science education.
mela-de-chorographia-latin-1880:
Pomponius Mela wrote the first geography in Latin to survive, in the first century of the Empire. De Chorographia, in Carl Frick's 1880 school text, gives Mela's three books on the world. Frick's edition prints the spare Latin in a clean, worked form.

Mela walks the coasts of the known world, land by land, naming seas, towns, tribes, and wonders. His earth is a ring of lands around a great sea, edged by strange peoples. The book is short, brisk, and full of the color of its age. It opens the Latin line of writing about the earth.
yeates-affidavit-nsa-1980:
The National Security Agency fought in court to keep 156 UFO reports sealed, and its sworn word is this file. The in camera affidavit of Eugene Yeates, dated October 9, 1980, was sworn in the case of CAUS against the NSA. Yeates was chief of the agency's Office of Policy.

He tells the judge, in a closed filing, why each of the reports must stay dark. The papers were communications intelligence tied to foreign air and spy craft. Freed at last in 2009, with black bars still in place, the affidavit is the core file of NSA UFO secrecy. It shows the agency guarding its silence by law.
zollner-transcendental-physics-1880:
Johann Zollner claimed a fourth span of space in Transcendental Physics, his book in English from 1880. Zollner was a chief of star lore at Leipzig. He sat with Slade, a famed seer, and saw knots tied in sealed cords, rings passed through wood, and goods moved in ways no hand in our space could work, he swore.

A fourth span, with souls in it, is his bold key. Peers cried fraud and shame. Fans hailed a new age of science. The book is the row's most famed flash point. Its claims still spark heat.
wood-order-zeuglodontia-nature-1880:
Searles Wood makes a bold claim for the sea serpent in his Nature note of 1880. Wood was a sage of old life forms. Ships oft told of a great long necked beast in far seas. He holds the beast could be a zeuglodon. Such whales of old ages had snake like frames. Thought long dead, one may yet live in deep seas men can't sweep.

His note is brief, grave, and writ for sages, not crowds. It gave the serpent a place in the tree of life. The row it sparked ran for years. It is a key text of that row.
grimm-teutonic-mythology-stallybrass-188:
Jacob Grimm, best known for the tales he gathered with his brother, built this vast study of German myth over many years. James Steven Stallybrass turned it into English in four parts from 1880 to 1888. Grimm worked from old poems, laws, and folk speech. He spent years in the work, and the notes grew to a vast heap.

The study traces gods, heroes, beasts, and rites across the old German world. Rune lore runs through it, tied to names, charms, and carved signs. Nearly all later work on German myth starts here, and its notes still guide those who study the north.
scheele-air-and-fire-1780:
Carl Wilhelm Scheele was a Swedish apothecary who built a great lab life on a small wage. His work on air and fire came out in German in 1777, then in English in 1780. He did his best work in small towns, far from the great schools.

Scheele found the gas we now call oxygen on his own, and named it fire air. He printed his claim late, so the fame went to men who spoke first in public. The book is his own record, and it shows a fine hand at trials.
hodgkin-italy-invaders-vol-1-1880:
Thomas Hodgkin published Italy and Her Invaders, Volume 1, in 1880. Hodgkin tells the story of the barbarian invasions of Italy from the Italian side. This volume covers the Visigoths, Alaric's sack of Rome in 410, and the Vandals. The fall of the Western Empire unfolds through Italian eyes.

Hodgkin writes with deep learning and humane sympathy for all sides. He studies church, law, and daily life beside battles and kings. The full work grew to eight volumes over many years. It became the English classic of the invasions period. Readers who want the end of Rome told fully and fairly start with Hodgkin. His patience rewards theirs.
wallace-island-life-1880:
In Island Life, published in 1880, Wallace asks why islands hold such strange mixes of plants and animals. He draws on his years in Malaysia and on reports from sailors and collectors worldwide. Islands, he argues, are natural test cases for how life spreads and changes. The book grew from the same travels as his Malay Archipelago.

Wallace weighs two answers: creatures rafted or flew across seas, or old land bridges once joined now-split lands. He uses ice ages, sea depth, and fossils to test each island case by case. His work founded island biogeography and still guides the study of island species.
legge-religions-of-china-1880:
James Legge, the Scottish missionary and Oxford professor who translated the Chinese classics, published The Religions of China in 1880. The book gives his comparative account of the faiths he had lived among for thirty years in Hong Kong. Legge writes as both scholar and former missionary.

He treats Confucianism as a moral and ancestral system, Taoism as a teaching decayed into magic, and Buddhism as an import that reshaped China. His judgments favor Confucius, whose works he had spent his life translating. The book shows Victorian sinology at its most learned and most confident. Readers can watch a fine scholar wrestle with faiths not his own.
hershon-talmudic-miscellany-1880:
Paul Isaac Hershon was a Polish Jewish scholar who settled in London and translated rabbinic texts for English readers. His Talmudic Miscellany, published in 1880, gathers a thousand and one extracts from the Talmud, the Midrashim, and the Kabbalah. The book appeared in Trubner's Oriental Series.

Hershon orders his extracts by theme: prayer, ethics, folklore, law, and the sayings of famous rabbis. A gentile reader could browse rabbinic wisdom here without Hebrew or a guide through the vast originals. The miscellany became a classic of its series and a quiet bridge between Jewish and Christian readers.
sixth-and-seventh-books-of-moses-1880:
The Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses, in this 1880 English edition prepared under Johann Scheibel's name, is a German folk grimoire ascribed to Moses. A grimoire is a handbook of spells, seals, and conjurations for practical use. No book of spells traveled further in American folk practice.

Its pages give seals, psalms, and formulas for healing, finding treasure, binding enemies, and turning luck. German settlers carried it into Pennsylvania Dutch country, and from there it passed into African-American hoodoo practice. Conjure workers treated the book itself as a power object, kept wrapped and hidden like a weapon.
knights-of-pythias-illustrated-1880:
Knights of Pythias Illustrated, issued by publisher E A Cook in 1880, printed the ritual of the Knights of Pythias with pictures. The Knights were a fraternal order founded during the Civil War, built on the story of Damon and Pythias and their famed friendship. Cook sold such books to readers eager to see inside secret lodges.

Inside are the forms for opening a lodge, admitting members, and giving the degrees, shown step by step. Signs, grips, and emblems appear with the words said to go with them. The book served critics of secret orders, curious readers, and anyone who wanted the hidden work of the lodge in plain print.
gaius-institutes-muirhead-1880:
James Muirhead published his translation of The Institutes of Gaius in 1880. Gaius, a Roman law teacher, wrote the Institutes around 160 CE as a textbook for students. The text was lost for centuries and recovered in 1816 from a scraped parchment in Verona.

Gaius sorted all law under persons, things, and actions, a scheme that law teaching used for a thousand years. His plain style and clear order made Roman law learnable, and Justinian's own Institutes copied his plan. Muirhead, a Scottish professor of law, added notes for English students. The translation gives modern readers the Roman law school's own starting point, in the form that taught lawyers for a millennium.
koch-etiology-traumatic-infective-diseas:
Robert Koch was a German country doctor who became a founder of bacteriology, the study of bacteria. In 1878 he published his research on wound infections in German. W. Watson Cheyne translated it for the New Sydenham Society, and the English version appeared in 1880.

Koch injected animals and traced which bacteria caused each kind of wound infection. He showed that specific germs, including the anthrax bacillus, produce specific diseases. His careful methods for growing and staining bacteria became standard lab practice. The work helped prove the germ theory and shaped how doctors hunt disease causes today.
james-washington-square-1880:
Henry James published Washington Square in 1880, building it from an anecdote a friend had told him at dinner. James set it in the New York of his childhood, in a house on Washington Square like his grandmother's. He considered it one of his most perfectly made works.

Catherine Sloper is a plain, shy heiress with a large fortune and a brilliant, cold father. When the handsome fortune hunter Morris Townsend courts her, Dr. Sloper forbids the match and threatens to disinherit her. Catherine must choose between obedience and the only love offered her. The tragedy unfolds in drawing rooms, almost in whispers. James called the story's design flawless, and its quiet ending still stings.
lanier-science-english-verse-1880:
Sidney Lanier published The Science of English Verse in 1880, built from lectures he gave at Johns Hopkins. Lanier was a Confederate veteran, a lawyer, and above all a musician: he played flute in Baltimore's Peabody orchestra. He brought a trained ear to a field ruled by counting syllables.

Lanier argues that verse is a kind of music and should be scanned in bars, like a score. Rhythm, pitch, and tone-color in speech get separate, careful treatment, with examples from Shakespeare onward. He treats bad verse as bad music and good verse as sound organized by law. The book is the first systematic American prosody, and working poets still consult it. Lanier died the next year, at thirty-nine.
shabistari-gulshan-i-raz-whinfield-1880:
Mahmud Shabistari was a Persian poet of Tabriz. In 1317 he answered seventeen questions on Sufi doctrine in verse, and he called the poem Gulshan-i Raz, the Rose Garden of Mystery. E. H. Whinfield published his English version in 1880, with an introduction and notes drawn from the great commentary of Lahiji. The Persian text pages are left out of this copy; the English matter is complete.

Question by question, Shabistari treats the self, the heart, the beloved, wine, and the tavern of ruin as signs of the soul's road to God. His answers became the pocket summa of Persian Sufism. Students memorized the couplets for six centuries. Whinfield's version was the first door into the garden for English readers.
acosta-natural-moral-history-markham-vol:
José de Acosta, a Spanish Jesuit who spent years in Peru, published his Historia natural y moral de las Indias in 1590. Volume one here is Clements R Markham's Hakluyt Society edition of 1880, built on Edward Grimston's English translation of 1604. Acosta set out to describe the New World whole: its skies, lands, plants, and peoples.

His natural history reasons about winds, climates, and species with a scholar's care and a traveler's eyes. His moral history turns to the customs and beliefs of the native peoples. Acosta even framed an early theory of how humans first reached the Americas. The work became the first broad natural history and ethnography of the New World.

Volume two completes Markham's 1880 edition of José de Acosta's Natural and Moral History of the Indies. The Spanish work of 1590, in Grimston's English of 1604, joined two surveys in one: the nature of the Americas and the life of their peoples. Acosta wrote from long residence in Peru and wide reading of reports.

The second volume carries his account of native religion, government, and custom to its close. He treats the peoples of Mexico and Peru as nations with laws, rites, and histories of their own. That respect, rare in his century, gives the book lasting worth. With volume one, it forms the first systematic survey of the New World.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol3-1880:
Hering's Guiding Symptoms reached its third volume in 1880, one more shelf of the ten-volume materia medica. The editorial team working from Constantine Hering's notes kept his system intact. Remedies appear in alphabetical order across the set, each with its full train of symptoms.

Mind, head, eyes, and the rest of the body each get their own sections within an entry. Odd and striking signs, the ones homeopaths call characteristic, stand out by their marks. Readers use the set as a court of appeal when smaller remedy books disagree, and Volume III does its share of that settling.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol4-1880:
By its fourth volume, from 1880, Hering's Guiding Symptoms had settled into the shape prescribers relied on. Each remedy entry moves through the body in a fixed order, so a reader always knows where to look. Marks of differing weight point to the signs worth trusting most.

Constantine Hering died the year the volume appeared, leaving his notes to students who kept the work going. What they printed came from provings, tests in which healthy people took a drug and noted each change. Volume IV shows the method at full stretch, a vast card index of symptoms bound as a book.
classical-poetry-japanese-chamberlain-18:
Basil Hall Chamberlain studied The Classical Poetry of the Japanese in 1880, the first systematic English treatment of the subject. His pioneering work translates poems from the Manyoshu and the Kokinshu, the great early anthologies. Chamberlain explains forms like the tanka while letting the poems themselves persuade the reader.

Courtly love, war, travel, and the seasons pass in verses of thirty-one syllables. Chamberlain wrote when Japan was just opening to the West, and his sympathy set the tone for later study. The book remains a graceful first door into Japan's classical verse for English readers.
brett-legends-and-myths-of-the-aborigina:
William Henry Brett was a missionary who spent decades among the native peoples of British Guiana, learning their languages and listening to their stories. In 1880 he published the legends and myths he had gathered, one of the first such collections from the region.

The tales tell of Makonaima, the great spirit, of a world flood, and of the origins of the sun, moon, and animals. Arawak and Carib traditions stand side by side, showing both shared roots and tribal differences. Brett recorded stories that elders feared would die with them. His book remains a basic source for Guiana mythology.
marsh-odontornithes-1880:
Othniel Charles Marsh, a Yale professor and fossil hunter, published Odontornithes in 1880. The monograph describes extinct birds with teeth, found in the chalk beds of Kansas. Marsh was Cope's great rival in the race for fossils.

The toothed birds, like Hesperornis and Ichthyornis, mixed bird traits with reptile traits. Their jaws held real teeth, and their bones told of swimming and flight long ago. For Darwin's supporters, they were gold: a clear link between reptiles and birds. Darwin himself praised Marsh's finds as strong support for evolution. Full measures and plates record the Kansas finds in detail.
plos-pone-0003380:
Stefano Volinia and co-authors hunted for hidden cancer genes in this 2008 paper. Some cancer genes act only when both copies of the gene are lost. Single tests miss such genes, since one working copy can hide the damage. The team combined several kinds of gene damage into one genome-wide search.

They joined data on changed amino acids, broken reading frames, and deleted genes. Looking at the combined signals across more than twenty thousand genes flagged new suspects. The method aims at cancer genes that act in a recessive way. Its list gives other labs fresh targets to test in tumors.
plos-pone-0003480:
Lutz Bornmann, Gerlind Wallon, and Anna Ledin graded grant peer review in this 2008 study. Peer review claims to pick the best science and the best scientists. They tested that claim on two European Molecular Biology Organization programmes. Both pick fellows and young investigators by committee.

The authors checked whether chosen applicants really proved best later. Their analysis probed the selection process programme by programme. Findings like these matter to every funder using expert panels. If review misses top talent, the whole funding system needs repair. Funders across Europe use panels like these for most of their awards.
plos-pone-0003580:
José N. Boada and co-authors proposed a simple drug scoring method in this 2008 paper. Several math models exist to weigh a drug's risks against benefits. Their use in practice has stayed rather limited. The team's aim was a model anyone could apply easily.

Their method, called NEAR, stands for net efficacy adjusted for risk. It builds on the share of patients who respond to treatment. One clear number may help doctors balance benefit and harm. Simple tools stand a better chance of reaching daily prescribing. Doctors weigh such trade-offs daily, often with no clear rule to guide them.
plos-pone-0003680:
Vikram Mehraj, Juanita Hatcher, Saeed Akhtar, and colleagues published this public health study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Intestinal parasites cause illness worldwide, above all where poverty and poor hygiene prevail. The team surveyed children in an urban slum of Karachi, Pakistan.

They measured how common parasitic infection was among the children. They also recorded which household and living factors went with higher risk. The results point prevention toward clean water, hygiene, and the crowded conditions that let parasites spread from child to child in poor districts. Such surveys guide where aid and clean water should go first.
plos-pone-0003780:
Alessandro Esposito, Teresa Tiffert, Jakob M. A. Mauritz, and colleagues published this malaria imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2008. While growing inside a red blood cell, Plasmodium falciparum eats up to eighty percent of the cell's hemoglobin. That is far more than the parasite needs for food. A model proposed a reason tied to cell balance.

The authors used FRET imaging to measure hemoglobin concentration inside infected red cells. Their readings test the model of how the parasite manages its host cell's contents. The work probes why malaria consumes its host's cargo so far beyond its own needs.
plos-pone-0003880:
Alexandre Leroux and Luis A. Rokeach examined a channel that moves proteins in cells in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns the translocon, a pore in the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum. New proteins pass through it to enter the secretory path. The pore has three main parts, named Sec61 alpha, beta, and gamma in mammals.

Unlike the other parts, the beta part can be lost without stopping transport. The authors tested whether beta parts from unlike species can swap and still work. They found that only its membrane-spanning part is needed for that swap. The result narrows which piece of beta matters most for the pore.
plos-pone-0003980:
Kevin A. Judge and Vanessa L. Bonanno looked for weapons on male field crickets in 2008. Fighting crickets are classic models for male aggression research. They are also famous from cricket fights in Chinese culture. Yet field crickets were not known to carry male weapons.

Their PLOS ONE article reports sexually dimorphic weaponry in a fighting cricket. Males carry structures that females lack, shaped for combat. Such weapons evolve where males fight over mates. Finding them in a model group reopens questions about cricket contests. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004080:
Imma Raurell, Montserrat Codina, David Casagolda, and co-authors studied a protein mutated in inherited Alzheimer's in 2008. Presenilin1 is part of the gamma-secretase complex that cuts proteins. Mutations in it cause familial Alzheimer's disease. Presenilin1 is made as one piece, then split into two linked parts.

Their PLOS ONE article separates the protein's effects on beta-catenin signaling. Some effects need gamma-secretase activity and some do not. Beta-catenin with Tcf-4 switches genes on in that pathway. Untangling the effects clarifies what Alzheimer's mutations disturb beyond cutting. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check. Each claim in it can be checked in the full text that sits with this record.
plos-pone-0004180:
Xiaoxing Huang and colleagues published this vaccine study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Vaccines given through mucosal surfaces, such as the nose or mouth, can block viruses where they first enter the body. The team compared two vaccinia-based vectors head to head: MVA, a well-known weakened strain, and MVTT, a novel version that can still copy itself.

They measured the neutralising antibody levels each vector produced after mucosal vaccination. They report that MVTT was superior to MVA, inducing higher levels of these virus-blocking antibodies. The comparison informs the design of vaccines delivered without needles.
plos-pone-0004280:
Daniel Wolfe, Anne Buboltz, and Eric Harvill published this microbiology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Recognising bacterial lipopolysaccharide through Toll-like receptor 4 is a key step in building protection against several Gram-negative germs. B. pertussis causes whooping cough itself. Two Bordetella species, close relatives of the whooping cough germ, trigger robust TLR4 responses that immunity requires.

The team show that Bordetella parapertussis stimulates TLR4 inefficiently, and that this weakness lets it avoid host immunity. A quiet knock at the immune system's door, it seems, lets this pathogen slip inside. Weak sensing, in this case, is the pathogen's best disguise.
plos-pone-0004380:
Acute respiratory distress syndrome, called ARDS, is a severe lung failure. It can follow infection or injury and often needs intensive care. Reform talk filled the files that year, as the government weighed the Dulles team's harsh grades for the CIA.

A memcon lets later readers sit in on a talk they could not attend: who spoke, what was asked, what was left open. So the talk could guide later work, each point is set down while its weight is still clear. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1861-d80:
On 10 September 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote a second letter to Charles Francis Adams. It is document 80 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The habit of paired letters served a clerical end: one point per paper. It also served a human one, since Adams could act on each at its own speed. The pair shows the Secretary's office at its most neat under wartime strain. The clerks who kept these files gave the record the clean order it still has. A clear order to the record serves readers a century and a half later.
frus-1861-d180:
Writing on 18 September 1861, William H. Seward sent a letter to Carl Schurz in Madrid. It is document 180 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Enclosed papers gave an envoy proof and text to lay before a court. Schurz could use such matter in talks at Madrid the same week. The letter with its pack of papers shows diplomacy supplied like a brief for a case at law. Papers sent with a letter often held the texts of laws or notes for the envoy's use. A brief fit for a case at law is a fair image of the envoy's whole craft.
frus-1861-d280:
4 July 1861 is stamped on a letter Seward got from Mr. Haldeman. The printed record keeps it as Document 280 in the President's message volume for 1861. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d80:
Dated 13 June 1862, a report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London went to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 80 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d180:
Two Seward dispatches to London are dated 3 November 1862, and the first of them is Document 180 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Both went to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister to Britain.

Early November brought the British cabinet to its choice on the French truce plan. London was close to saying no, which would leave France to act alone or drop the scheme. Seward's mail in these days armed Adams for the final round of talks. This letter is one strand of the pressure and patience that kept Britain neutral. The State Department printed the London mail in full for Congress, enclosures and all.
frus-1862-d280:
On 22 May 1862 William L. Dayton sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a report printed as Document 280 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton was the American minister in Paris, reporting on his post.

Late May found the war's focus on Richmond, where McClellan's advance had slowed to a siege pace. In Paris, the question of the hour was whether France would act with Britain on the American war or wait. Dayton's reports tracked that question through court and ministry talk. This one belongs to the quiet weeks before the summer's storms. A steamer's sailing day set the legation's week, and Dayton wrote against that clock.
frus-1862-d380:
Cassius Clay, the American minister in Russia, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 January 1862, opening the Russian file in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume as Document 380.

Russia was the great power most friendly to the Union in these years, and the St. Petersburg post carried a warmth the London and Paris files lack. Clay, a Kentucky abolitionist serving as envoy, reported from a court that wished the Union well. His early 1862 letters set the tone for the volume's calmest channel. Prince Gorchakov, Russia's foreign minister, made his government's sympathy for the Union plain. The Russian route was the longest in the file, crossing an ocean and then half of Europe.
frus-1862-d480:
On 16 September 1862 James E. Harvey wrote from Lisbon to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is Document 480 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Harvey wrote the day before Antietam, though no word of the battle could reach him for weeks. His subject was Portugal: its court's temper, its port rules, and its place in the Atlantic war of cruisers and blockaders. Reports written in such ignorance of home events have their own honesty; they show what a post knew and feared on its own evidence. Seward read them all before shaping his autumn answers to Europe. The letter keeps the Portuguese thread of that story intact.
frus-1862-d580:
On 7 September 1862 James Watson Webb sent this report from Rio de Janeiro to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 580 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the annual message.

Webb wrote ten days before Antietam, in a hemisphere where the battle could not be known for many weeks. His subject was Brazil as he found it: its court's policy, its ports' practice, and the Union's standing there. Reports written in that isolation had to stand on the minister's own judgment, which in Webb's case was never in short supply. Seward read them for the southern facts of his global brief, and the September letter supplied them for the autumn file.
frus-1862-d680:
On 25 September 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to a Mr. Blatchford. The letter is document 680 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, set between the China file and the Egypt papers. Unlike most letters in the volume, it was not sent to an envoy posted abroad.

Seward's desk work ranged far past the great powers. Letters to men outside the legations still formed part of the State Department's record, and this one was kept and printed with the rest. It gives a glimpse of the smaller business that crossed a secretary's desk in wartime, next to the fate of nations.
frus-1863p1-d80:
Charles Francis Adams closed a three-letter day with this dispatch of 13 February 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 80 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The same date also drew a letter from Seward's side of the file, so the pens crossed that day on the Atlantic. Adams's third sheet rounds out his 13 February set. His winter mail kept a steady theme: Britain calm, the South's friends busy, the Union's cause held by care and facts. This letter is the last word of that day from London, filed with the rest.
frus-1863p1-d180:
Reports like this one carried London news to Washington. This one went from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 May 1863, and it is document 180 of the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Mail crossed the Atlantic by steamship, taking roughly ten days or more each way. News in a dispatch like this one was already old when Seward read it, yet it guided his next orders. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d280:
On 4 September 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this dispatch from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 280 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Read in sequence, these reports show a diplomat testing how far he could push a stronger power without provoking a second war. That balance was the heart of Adams's whole mission. It belongs to the tense autumn when the fate of two Confederate ironclad rams in British yards hung in the balance. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d380:
Washington's business with Britain on 31 January 1863 included this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The paper is document 380 of the 1863 volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

Britain had claimed neutral rights at sea, while the Union navy stopped British ships suspected of aiding the South. The friction from those seizures runs through this whole exchange. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d480:
W. Hunter, chief clerk of the State Department directed a letter to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington on 27 April 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d580:
Document 580, dated 30 June 1863, records a letter from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons to William H. Seward, Secretary of State. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d680:
On 5 December 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent fresh word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The dispatch is document 680 in Foreign Relations of the United States, the printed record of Civil War era talks with other nations.

December brought the close of a hard year. Gettysburg and Vicksburg had raised Union hopes, yet British choices still mattered a great deal. Seward's job was to keep Britain neutral and to guard American trade and rights at sea. This letter is one link in that chain. It lets readers watch policy move in real time, not in a later summary.
plos-pbio-0000080:
Prabhat S. Kunwar, Michelle Starz-Gaiano, Roland J. Bainton, and others studied germ cell movement in the fruit fly for PLOS Biology in 2003. Germ cells form far from the gonad, the organ where they must end up. They cross a sheet of gut cells to get there, guided by signals.

The team found that a receptor called Tre1 steers that crossing. Tre1 belongs to a large family of receptors that sense cues outside the cell. Without its guidance, germ cells fail to pass through the gut wall as they should. The work shows how a single signal can direct a key step in building the reproductive system. That step is shared, in broad form, by many animals.
plos-pbio-0020280:
Vitali Matyash, Eugeni V. Entchev, Fanny Mende, and their team studied worm dormancy in PLOS Biology in 2004. When food runs out, young C. elegans worms can enter diapause, a paused state called the dauer stage. They can wait there for months until times improve.

A hormone made from sterols, the fat family that includes cholesterol, controls entry into that pause. The study shows the hormone works by switching on a chain of genes in sequence. Naming the hormone signal fills a long-standing gap in worm biology. It also links this worm's survival trick to steroid hormones in other animals, including humans, where similar signals time growth and reproduction.
plos-pbio-0020380:
Damien Devos, Svetlana Dokudovskaya, Frank Alber, and a large team compared two cell structures in PLOS Biology in 2004. Coated vesicles are small sacs that ferry cargo between cell compartments. Nuclear pore complexes are the gates through the nucleus membrane. The two look different, yet their parts share a common architecture.

Shared shape suggests a shared origin deep in evolution, when early cells were building inner compartments. The authors lay out the structural kinship piece by piece. That kind of deep link helps explain how complex cells arose from simpler ones. It also predicts that lessons from one structure, like how its coat bends a membrane, will apply to the other.
plos-pone-0000080:
Zhihua Jiang, Jennifer J. Michal, Galen A. Williams, and their team checked two obesity drug targets in PLOS ONE in 2006. The targets are a hormone called UCN3 and its receptor CRHR2, which help control appetite and stress responses. The team compared the genes across species to judge whether animal results might apply to people.

Drug targets that behave the same in test animals and in humans are far more likely to pay off. Cross-species checks like this one sort promising targets from traps early. The appetite system is full of targets that worked in mice and failed in people. A careful filter at the gene level saves years of wasted effort and guides safer trials.
plos-pone-0000180:
James O. Lloyd-Smith published this statistics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Outbreak data are often highly overdispersed: most cases cause few infections, while a few cause many. The negative binomial distribution captures that spread through a dispersion parameter, and the author presents a way to estimate it by maximum likelihood.

Getting that parameter right changes how superspreading is measured and how outbreaks are modeled. The method is aimed at infectious disease data, where overdispersion is the rule. It gives epidemiologists a more reliable handle on one of the key numbers describing how a disease spreads.
plos-pone-0000280:
Saman K. Hashmi, Maria B. Afridi, Kanza Abbas, and colleagues published this public health study from Pakistan in PLOS ONE in 2007. It examines factors associated with adherence to anti-hypertensive treatment, whether patients with high blood pressure actually keep taking their medicines. Poor adherence is one of the main reasons blood pressure stays uncontrolled.

High blood pressure is silent, so patients often stop pills they feel no benefit from. The authors identify what helps or hinders sticking with treatment in this setting. Findings like these guide clinics in supporting patients, since an untaken drug cannot prevent a stroke.
plos-pone-0000380:
Yu-Tsueng Liu and Dennis A. Carson presented a new laboratory approach in PLOS ONE in 2007 for finding breakpoints in cancer genomes. A breakpoint is a spot where a chromosome has broken and rejoined, an error that can drive cancer growth. Tumor samples are usually mixed with normal cells, and that normal DNA hides the breaks.

The method aims to pinpoint breakpoints even when normal DNA is present in the sample. Finding exact break locations matters because they often reveal fused genes or lost control regions that push a cell toward cancer. A cleaner way to locate them could sharpen diagnosis and help match patients to treatments aimed at their tumor's specific errors.
plos-pone-0000480:
Luisa Bernardinelli and colleagues tested a gene's link to multiple sclerosis in a distinctive population, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The gene is ACCN1, which makes an ion channel that senses acid in tissue. The study population lived in central east Sardinia, an island whose long-isolated communities are prized for genetic studies.

Multiple sclerosis, where the immune system strips insulation from nerves, clusters on Sardinia at unusually high rates. Isolated populations concentrate genetic signals, so an association found there can reveal risk factors hidden elsewhere. The team reported an association between ACCN1 and the disease in this population, adding a candidate to the list of MS risk genes.
plos-pone-0000580:
Thomas P. Gosden and Erik I. Svensson studied a mating system where females come in several forms, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Female sexual polymorphism means females of one species have distinct types, often differing in color. The team measured the fecundity consequences of male mating harassment in the wild: how persistent male attention affects each type's egg production.

Harassment is a real cost of being common and attractive; rare female types may escape it, which helps keep several types in the population. Measuring egg output in the wild ties that theory to fitness. The study is a neat test of frequency-dependent selection maintaining variety.
plos-pone-0000680:
Denis G. Pelli and Katharine A. Tillman separated three routes to recognizing words, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Object recognition research has long debated two routes: seeing the whole at once, or assembling parts. Context offers a third route, since an object can be guessed from its surroundings. Words are objects too, and how we recognize them is the core question of reading research.

Their title claims a triple dissociation, evidence that parts, wholes, and context each contribute separately. Do fast readers lean on letters, word shapes, or context most? A clean separation of the three helps explain skilled reading, and it may clarify what breaks down in reading disorders.
plos-pone-0000780:
Robert A. Kleps, Terrell C. Myers, Romuald N. Lipcius and colleagues used a physics tool to find a chemistry difference between the sexes of a marine invertebrate. Hormone levels are generally accepted as the main cause of sexual dimorphism, the differing forms of males and females. Levels of small metabolites also differ between men and women, in circulating amino acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and within brain tissue.

Their method was phosphorus-31 nuclear magnetic resonance, which detects phosphorus-bearing compounds. The title reports a sex-specific metabolite identified this way. A molecule found in one sex only hints that development's chemistry differs beyond hormones, in creatures far simpler than humans.
plos-pone-0000880:
Sunhwan Jo, Taehoon Kim and Wonpil Im presented an automated builder and database for protein and membrane systems, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Computer simulations of membrane proteins can reveal how they work at the atomic level. Setting up a fair test system, though, is much harder than placing a normal protein in water.

Their tool builds a realistic protein set into a membrane for molecular dynamics simulations, the physics based movies of atoms in motion. A shared database of ready systems saves each lab from starting over. Tools like this quietly speed up drug and basic research on the proteins that sit in cell membranes.
plos-pone-0000980:
Freddie-Jeanne Richard, David Tarpy and Christina Grozinger measured how mating quantity reshapes honey bee queen physiology, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Mating changes female insects deeply, and in honey bee queens the changes are permanent. Queens mate with many males in a brief window early in life, then begin laying eggs.

The team varied insemination quantity and tracked what changed inside the queen. Knowing which shifts follow mating itself, and which follow the amount, helps explain queen health and colony performance. Beekeepers depend on queens that stay productive for seasons. The study breaks a once in a lifetime event into parts that can be tested.
plos-pone-0001080:
Jason Barbour, Mariana Sauer, Elizabeth Sharp and colleagues studied people carrying both HIV and herpes simplex virus 2, in PLOS ONE in 2007. HIV is often acquired while other infections are already present. HSV-2, a common sexually transmitted virus, is one of the most frequent of those companions.

The team examined how HSV-2 status at the time of HIV acquisition affects the later clinical course and CD4 T cell patterns. Their title reports elevated CD4 counts in co-infected adults early in HIV infection, a direction that needs care in reading. Co-infection studies warn against treating HIV's course as set by HIV alone.
plos-pone-0001180:
Wheezing in infancy has been linked to lungs that work less well later in childhood. Christophe Delacourt and colleagues followed a group of asthmatic infants to test that link, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They focused on bronchial hyperresponsiveness, the tendency of airways to narrow too easily.

The team prospectively investigated how hyperresponsiveness relates to progressive impairment of lung function, following the children until age nine. Their study connects a measurable airway trait in infancy to lung performance years later. Such links help doctors judge which wheezy infants need the closest watch.
plos-pone-0001280:
In pond-dwelling Daphnia magna, genotypes differ in how well they compete and in how often they get infected. Florian Altermatt and Dieter Ebert tested whether those two traits go together in natural populations, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The cost of resistance hypothesis predicts that resistant genotypes pay for their resistance with lower fitness when uninfected.

The authors report, as their title states, that genotype-specific competitive ability does not correlate with infection in the natural populations studied. That null result still teaches: a popular theory prediction failed in the field. It pushes theory toward the mess of real populations.
plos-pone-0001380:
Richard Haber and Warren Browner wrote a 2007 PLOS ONE study on low phosphate in the blood of malaria patients. Low phosphate shows up in 40 to 60 percent of acute malaria cases. It also shows up in other states marked by high fever. The pair asked whether fever itself might be the cause.

They looked back at records for all adults found to have malaria in their data set. By weighing fever against other traits, they tested the link in a direct way. Sorting out this cause matters for care, since low phosphate can weaken muscles and breathing. The study gives doctors a clearer guide for when to check and treat it.
plos-pone-0001480:
Tihana Jovanic and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on an enzyme that starts gene changes in immune cells. The enzyme sparks changes in antibody genes by altering one DNA letter. Those changes come in two phases, one tied to DNA copying. The team placed the enzyme in a non immune cell line to test its reach.

They found it can spark both kinds of change in test DNA rings that do not copy. That widens the view of how this enzyme can act. Since stray action by it can help cause cancers, sharp maps of its reach matter. The work refines a key step in how antibodies are honed.
plos-pone-0001580:
Nicolas Mathevon and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on birdsong in the rain forest. How song form is shaped by the place it must travel through is a key test of communication theory. Forest air bends sound, so forest birds should sing in ways that carry well there. The team studied a tropical bird's song in its own forest.

They tracked how the song's parts carry data as they move through the trees. Some cues fade fast while others hold up over range. That split shows which parts a mate or rival can truly use at a distance. It refines the rules for how habitats sculpt animal signals.
plos-pone-0001680:
Thomas Steiner and co-authors tuned a glowing protein's folding with a swapped building block, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Green fluorescent protein, GFP, glows under light and is a standard lab marker. Its folding and stability depend in part on proline. That amino acid's bonds can flip between two shapes, and its ring can pucker two ways.

The team replaced proline with fluoroproline, a fluorine-bearing version, to steer those shapes. The full text gives the protein variants, their glow, and their stability measurements. The study shows how one careful swap in a protein's parts list can retune its behavior. Synthetic biology can apply that method to enzymes and materials well beyond GFP.
plos-pone-0001780:
Lee R. Berger, Steven E. Churchill, Bonita De Klerk, and their co-authors reported small-bodied human fossils from Palau in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Surface collection and test excavation in limestone caves in Palau's rock islands, in Micronesia, produced fossil assemblages of small-bodied Homo sapiens. Some features looked primitive, of a kind thought to mark early members of the genus Homo.

The full text describes the bones, their cave context, and the size estimates. Small island humans recall the Flores 'hobbit' finds, and island dwarfing is a known response to isolation and scarce food. The Palau material lets researchers test how fast body size shrinks on islands, and it drew wide debate on how the bones should be interpreted.
plos-pone-0001880:
Dario Greco and colleagues took a broad look at what makes each human tissue distinct in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. A liver cell and a skin cell hold the same genes, yet each turns on its own set. Some genes run in all tissues for basic house tasks, while others run in just one or a few tissues.

By pooling gene activity data from many past studies, the team sorted genes into house-wide and tissue-tied groups. They then used those maps to judge how tissues relate to each other in health and in disease. Such maps help labs spot when a tissue has drifted from its true self, a hallmark of many ills.
plos-pone-0001980:
Ron Kerkhoven and co-authors warned of a hidden bias in gene chip studies, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Microarrays read the activity of thousands of genes at once, but samples often must be amplified first. One common method, based on the T7 primer, adds short stretches of six to ten letters to the start of each copied message.

Across more than six thousand arrays, the team found that probes matching those added stretches gave falsely high signals. As the title states, the primer is a source of bias and of variety between platforms. Labs that know the trap can clean old data and design better chips.
plos-pone-0002080:
Ming Li and co-authors found a two-part signal system a pig bacterium needs to cause severe disease, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Streptococcus suis serotype 2 has evolved into a highly infectious form. It caused two large outbreaks of human disease in China, marked by a toxic shock-like syndrome. How it causes such illness was still being worked out.

The system, called SalK/SalR, is a two-component signal pathway that senses the world and switches genes on. As the title states, it is essential for the full virulence of this invasive strain. Break that sensor, and a drug might disarm the bacterium without killing it outright.
plos-pone-0002180:
Semir Zeki, Oliver Hulme, and Barrie Roulston scanned the brains of people watching regular and irregular visual patterns, for a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The brain is quick to notice when a steady rhythm in what we see is broken. The team set out to find the neural systems that detect predictable timing and departures from it.

Using functional MRI, they watched brain activity while subjects viewed displays whose timing was either regular or irregular. The scans located the areas that respond to each kind of pattern. Knowing where the brain tracks regularity helps explain how we spot the odd event in a stream of sights.
plos-pone-0002280:
Maha Saeed and co-authors looked for surface proteins on the sexual stage of the malaria parasite, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The blood stages of Plasmodium falciparum display many varied, strongly immunogenic proteins on the red cells they infect. Far fewer studies had examined the gametocyte, the stage that mosquitoes pick up to spread malaria.

Using flow cytometry, the team probed the surface of red cells carrying gametocytes for parasite antigens. Finding such proteins matters because antibodies against them could block transmission to mosquitoes. Transmission-blocking targets are a distinct and hopeful front in malaria vaccine research.
plos-pone-0002380:
Led by Overney, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Leila S. Overney, Olaf Blanke, Michael H. Herzog, and others. Its subject is enhanced Temporal but Not Attentional Processing in Expert Tennis Players. In tennis, as in many disciplines of sport, fine spatio-temporal resolution is required to reach optimal performance.

While many studies on tennis have focused on anticipatory skills or decision making, fewer have studied the underlying visual perception abilities. What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002480:
Research by Finkelstein and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Myra Finkelstein, Victoria Bakker, Daniel F. Doak, and others. Its subject is evaluating the Potential Effectiveness of Compensatory Mitigation Strategies for Marine Bycatch. Conservationists are continually seeking new strategies to reverse population declines and safeguard against species extinctions.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002580:
Xiang and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Jinhua Xiang, James H. McLinden, Qing Chang, and others. Its subject is characterization of a Peptide Domain within the GB Virus C NS5A Phosphoprotein that Inhibits HIV Replication. GBV-C infection is linked to prolonged survival in HIV-infected people and GBV-C inhibits HIV replication in co-infection models.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002680:
Research from Naila O. Alieva and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers diversity and evolution of coral fluorescent proteins. The catalog record names Naila O. Alieva first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. GFP-like fluorescent proteins (FPs) are the key color determinants in reef-building corals (class Anthozoa. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002780:
Work by Jennifer Winter and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was comparative 3'UTR analysis allows identification of regulatory clusters that drive eph/ephrin expression in cancer cell lines. Authorship is credited in the record to Jennifer Winter and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Eph receptors are the largest family of receptor tyrosine kinases. The authors add a further point. Together with their ligands, the ephrins, they fulfill multiple biological functions. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002880:
Jian Liang, Wenjun Song, Gail Tromp and co-authors surveyed a whole gene family in PLOS ONE in 2008. The family makes CCCH zinc finger proteins, named for the pattern of atoms that grips zinc in each protein. Earlier work had cast some members as brakes on macrophage activation, the process that arms a key immune cell.

The authors combined a genome-wide survey with tests of gene activity to judge the family's role when macrophages switch on. That gives a fuller view than studying one gene at a time. Immunologists get a map of which family members may help calm or shape inflammation.
plos-pone-0002980:
Norbert Dahmen, Nina Manderscheid, Jana Helfrich and co-authors measured the fat signal visfatin in narcolepsy patients in 2008. Narcolepsy is a severe sleep disorder with excess daytime sleepiness, sudden muscle weakness called cataplexy, and a tendency toward obesity. Its main cause is loss of hypocretin-producing neurons, likely by immune attack.

Peripheral visfatin levels were elevated in patients, as the title states. Published in PLOS ONE, the finding connects a sleep disorder with a metabolic signal. It may help explain the weight gain so common in narcolepsy and guide further metabolic study of the condition.
plos-pone-0003080:
Ian Fiske, Emilio Bruna and Benjamin Bolker asked how sample size warps population growth estimates in 2008. Matrix models are widely used to study population dynamics and demography. How the number of sampled individuals influences the estimated growth rate, called lambda, was an important but overlooked issue.

Even unbiased estimates of birth and death rates can combine into biased growth estimates at small samples. Published in PLOS ONE, the analysis warns ecologists that small field samples flatter or sink a population's outlook by chance. Study design for rare species needs that correction. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003180:
John Richards, Beth McNally, Xianfeng Fang and colleagues study how tumour growth affects immune cell production in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Chronic tumour growth is well known to inactivate T cells and NK cells in function. It was less clear whether lymphopoiesis, the making of new lymphoid cells, is also affected. While analysing tumour effects on NK cell development, the team observed a broader pattern.
